context.text: Polycarp had been bishop of Smyrna for half a century and was the living link to the apostles: Irenaeus, who as a boy heard him teach, records that Polycarp had 'conversed with John and the others who had seen the Lord.' During a local persecution the crowd demanded the 'teacher of Asia.'

narrative.text: Brought into the stadium and pressed by the proconsul to swear by Caesar and curse Christ, the old man answered: 'Eighty-six years have I served Him, and He never did me wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' Refusing to be nailed to the pyre, 'He who gives me strength to endure the fire will grant me to remain in it unmoved', he prayed aloud, blessing God 'that You have counted me worthy of this day and hour,' and was burned, then stabbed.

The church of Smyrna's letter recounting his death, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, is the earliest detailed martyr-account outside the New Testament, and already shows the Church gathering the martyr's bones 'more precious than jewels' and keeping the 'birthday' of his martyrdom: the beginning of the cult of the saints and their relics.

significance.text: In Polycarp the apostolic generation's faith passes intact into the second century, sealed in blood. The Martyrdom's theology, the martyr as imitator of Christ, the relics honored, the annual commemoration, is the seed of the Orthodox veneration of saints.

uncertainty: The Martyrdom's date-notice points to February 23, most likely in 155 or 156 (some scholars argue 166–167); the year shown is the scholarly majority view.
